lesson.title: Choose the right denominator

lead.text: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX on a column use only its known values.
COALESCE(amount, 0) swaps an unknown for 0 before the aggregate sees it. That changes what they see.

steps.headline: An aggregate turns many rows into one value, using only the known values.

lead.text: The orders table has six rows, and one amount is unknown. Compare counting rows with counting a column.

reveal.text: You left out the unknown amount, so the column count came out one short of the row count. That gap is how a missing value shows.

queries.label: Count every order
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders;

queries.label: Count known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders;

steps.headline: Find the average amount for customer 3's orders.

queries.label: Known amounts only
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 3;

queries.label: Unknown counted as zero
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known, AVG(COALESCE(amount, 0)) AS mean FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 3;

workedSteps.text: AVG uses only the known amounts.
COALESCE(amount, 0) would count the unknown as 0 instead.

lead.text: SUM adds the known amounts. AVG divides that sum by the number of known amounts.

reveal.text: You divided by the known amounts only. The unknown amount neither adds to the total nor counts as an order.

queries.label: Keep missing separate
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders;

queries.label: Fill missing with zero
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(COALESCE(amount, 0)) AS total, AVG(COALESCE(amount, 0)) AS mean FROM orders;

lead.text: MIN and MAX pass over unknown values too. Filter first, then pick from the rows that are left.

reveal.text: You picked from the known amounts of the filtered rows. An unknown amount never stands in for a smallest value.

queries.label: All orders
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS minimum, MAX(amount) AS maximum FROM orders;

queries.label: Pending only
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS minimum, MAX(amount) AS maximum FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';

lead.text: Suppose WHERE leaves no rows at all. An aggregate query still returns a single row. Think about what a total of nothing means.

queries.label: Known orders
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders;

queries.label: No matches
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders WHERE amount > 100;

lesson.orientation: Use COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX while keeping missing values visible.
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Four pupils were asked how many books they read this month. Three answered 4, 6 and 8. The fourth did not answer.

intro.promise: By the end you'll know which rows each aggregate counts, and what an unknown value does to a total or an average.

recap.keyIdea: Aggregates use only known values: the denominator is the count of known amounts. COALESCE changes that by filling the gaps first.

blocks.text: You found an average of 6 from three answers and 48 from five known amounts. With no rows, a SUM came back NULL.

recap.nextHook: Next, summarise each group of rows separately.

questions.prompt: What does COUNT(amount) return for the original orders?
hints: Count known values in the column.
COUNT(amount) excludes the NULL row.
Order 106 has no known amount; inspect the amounts on all the other orders.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five rows have a non-NULL amount; order 106 is missing.

questions.onCorrect: 5. COUNT(amount) counts the known amounts, so the unknown one is left out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of rows, which COUNT(*) gives. COUNT(amount) skips the unknown amount.

questions.prompt: What is AVG(amount) for the original orders?
hints: Add only known amounts.
Use the count of known amounts as the denominator.
Evaluate 240 ÷ 5; NULL is outside this denominator.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known total is 240 across five known amounts: 240 ÷ 5 = 48.

questions.onCorrect: 48. SUM adds the known amounts, and AVG divides by how many there are.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by all six rows, as if the unknown amount were a zero.
That is the total. AVG divides it by the number of known amounts.

questions.prompt: What is MIN(amount) for pending orders?
hints: Filter to pending orders first.
Ignore the missing amount; do not replace it with zero.
The pending amounts are a known value on order 104 and NULL on order 106; only the known value participates.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Order 104 is the only pending order with a known amount; MIN is 40.

questions.onCorrect: 40. WHERE keeps the pending orders, and MIN ignores the unknown amount.

misconceptions.feedback: The unknown amount is not a zero. MIN ignores it.
That is the smallest amount over all orders. Filter to pending orders first.

questions.prompt: With no matching rows, type the value SUM(amount) returns in SQLite.
hints: No observed sum is different from a known zero sum.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: SQLite SUM(amount) returns NULL when there are no non-NULL input values, including an empty matching set. COUNT instead returns zero for an empty set.

questions.onCorrect: NULL. With no rows to add, SUM has no total to report, which is not the same as zero.

misconceptions.feedback: A total of zero would claim that rows were added up. With no rows there is no total.

questions.prompt: Known values are 10 and 30, with one NULL. What does AVG(value) return?
hints: The missing value does not add to the count.
Divide the known total by two.
Evaluate (10 + 30) ÷ 2; the missing observation is excluded.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: AVG uses the two known values: (10 + 30) ÷ 2 = 20.

questions.onCorrect: 20. The unknown value is out of the sum and the count, so it is 40 ÷ 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by three, counting the unknown value. AVG leaves it out.
That is the total. AVG divides it by the number of known values.

questions.prompt: What changes when you use AVG(COALESCE(amount, 0))?
hints: The replacement becomes an input value to AVG.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: COALESCE replaces each missing amount with zero before averaging. Those rows now contribute to the denominator, which can change the average.

questions.onCorrect: Missing amounts count as zeros. COALESCE replaces NULL before AVG sees it, so the count rises.

misconceptions.feedback: COALESCE fills the gap before AVG runs, so the gaps no longer disappear.
The values AVG reads change as well, so the average can change.

questions.prompt: What is the average number of books among the pupils who answered?
hints: Which pupils should count towards the average?
Add up the numbers that were reported.
Divide by the number of answers, not the number of pupils.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The answers are 4, 6 and 8. They add up to 18, and 18 ÷ 3 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. The pupil who did not answer adds nothing and is not counted. AVG treats an unknown value the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by all four pupils. The one who did not answer gave no number to include.

questions.prompt: Which one counts every row, including rows with an unknown amount?
hints: Which one does not look at a single column?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(amount) counts only rows where amount is known.

questions.onCorrect: COUNT(*) counts rows. Counting a column counts only its known values.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts known amounts only, so a row with an unknown amount is left out.
SUM adds amounts. It does not count rows.

questions.prompt: Why does AVG(amount) divide by one here, not two?
hints: How many of the two amounts are known?

acceptedIdeas: AVG counts only the known amounts.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One of the two amounts is unknown, and AVG leaves it out of both the sum and the count.

questions.onCorrect: AVG skips unknown values in the sum and in the count, so it divides by the known amounts only.

choices.label: AVG counts only the known amounts.
AVG treats the unknown amount as zero.

misconceptions.feedback: Then it would divide by both orders. AVG skips unknown values instead.
Nothing says it was cancelled. Its amount is simply not known.

questions.prompt: A column holds 5, NULL, 7 and 8. What does COUNT(column) return?
hints: Does COUNT(column) count the unknown value?
Count the values that are known.
Four rows, minus the unknown one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three of the four values are known, so COUNT(column) is three.

questions.onCorrect: 3. COUNT on a column counts known values, so the NULL is left out.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts rows. COUNT(column) skips the unknown value.
